The pattern to investigate is a trade-off. More analysis may avoid later work, but its own cost can outweigh the saving. The studies motivate questions; they do not establish that any proposed rule is new.

Study context and what is already known

1 · Define the problem

Make the same decision with less work.

A workflow is a set of tasks with prerequisites. Kahn’s algorithm identifies tasks that are ready. A priority rule chooses which ready task comes next. Our study concerns the cost of maintaining that rule, not the image processing itself. [E01] [E20]

Can one small change reduce the CPU time needed to construct a Montage task order, while preserving the reference method’s decisions?

Keep the graph and file sizes fixed; simulate one completion at a time. Use recorded task and file metadata. An ordinary computer is the implementation target—no image execution, GPU, or cloud deployment is part of this experiment. [E24]

Already known. Counting remaining users and updating priorities when one remains is in XLA. Reachability-based cleanup dependency removal appears in the 2007 workflow study. Neither is a new contribution by itself. [E20] [E08]

Where this fits in the field

Valid order is the foundation. Better execution order adds a scheduling objective. Cheaper priority maintenance keeps the chosen policy and reduces its overhead.

Dynamic topological ordering instead handles newly inserted graph edges. Parallel and streaming methods change the machine or input-access model. They provide context, but do not all belong in this experiment. [E03] [E05] [E06] [E13]

The complete 37-entry historical record is retained in the reference notes. Its relationships are labeled; chronological order alone does not prove inheritance.

New code comparison: a 25 September 2026 OpenXLA change [E29] already uses dense indices and shared ranges while claiming unchanged scheduling decisions. Treat representation reuse as prior art, not an untouched idea.

Research questions

What could be worth investigating?

These questions start from the evidence. They do not supply an algorithm or certify a research gap.

Check an idea before calling it new

Search the operation, not just “Kahn”: memory-aware list scheduling, last-use analysis, cleanup dependency reduction, incremental priority maintenance, and task-graph transformation. Trace the closest paper’s references and inspect its code where available.

Compare the changed operation, assumptions, guarantee, and total measured cost. A missing search result is not proof of absence. A useful result may be small, but it needs a genuine difference and a competent baseline.

4 · Plan a small test

A narrow claim needs a fair comparison.

Primary outcome

Total ordering time

Include the modification’s initialization, searches, grouping and queue preparation—not just the final loop.

One explanatory outcome

The operation you target

For a counter-focused change, count actual counter updates. Select the measure before the final benchmark.

Time saved = reference total time − proposed total time

Correctness is required. Preserve prerequisites, the priority formula and tie-breaking. A valid but different order does not demonstrate equivalence. Lower bookkeeping counts do not prove a runtime gain.

Use competent controls. Compare the modified implementation with the same-policy parent and its strongest relevant simple alternative. Use full recomputation as a correctness check—not the only performance baseline. Add one ablation that removes only your change.

Keep the benchmark small. Develop on the 58- and 310-task Montage 2MASS instances; then evaluate on the 103-, 619-, 748-, 1,312-, 1,738- and 4,846-task instances. Freeze versions and input hashes before measurement. These are documented workloads, not performance results. [E24]

Reinitialize mutable state for every run, alternate method order, and retain all valid timing observations. Report medians, variability, absolute savings and slowdowns for every input. Timing repeats are not additional independent workflows.

Include a few tiny correctness cases and one no-benefit case. A single task can confirm eligibility; overlapping consumers and equal priorities test less obvious errors.

Semester 1. Reproduce the closest method, profile the development traces, derive one change and review its nearest prior art. Freeze the design only after that pilot.

Semester 2. Run the declared comparisons, explain successes and regressions, and finish the thesis with reproducible code and inputs.

Earlier notes




A useful thesis can make a modest improvement. Its strength comes from a clear difference, a sound argument and an experiment that could prove it wrong.




Evidence and review limits


Yes, as a working evidence map—not as proof of exhaustive coverage or novelty. The refresh ends on 15 October 2026, not the end of the year. Keep later searches open until proposal submission.


What holds up
Side-by-side models, code provenance, counterexamples and local correctness tests help distinguish a small improvement from a renamed existing method.
What still blocks approval
Some records are abstract-only. The original search history is incomplete, full benchmark inputs have not been run, and the students have not yet specified a tested new rule.


Corrections that affect the thesis
IssueHow to use the evidence now


XLA snapshots were easy to confuse.The predecessor already has incremental priorities; dense indexing belongs to the September 2026 revision. Compare exact snapshots, not an outdated caricature.


Relevant tracking work was missing.Read Horizons, including its CPU-only dry runs and unfavorable threshold result.


Memory models could be conflated.Compare edge-output memory with shared-output pebbling before transferring a proof or complexity claim.


Recent work changes different decisions.LATTICE and MoSAIC are 2026 preprints, not evidence that our exact-order problem has been solved—or that it remains open.


Version families could look like independent confirmations.XLA versions, LRC versions and the Fradet research line have explicit family labels. A video or local test is not another primary experiment.




Search and selection record
This is a retrospective audit plus a targeted update. The original selection process cannot be reconstructed completely. The search log records the queries executed in this audit; it is not a complete database export or a PRISMA flow diagram.
Include work about fixed-order maintenance, dependency metadata, file lifetimes, close graph reductions, and competing memory models. Keep direct methods separate from contextual scheduling optimizers.
Do not exclude by result. Favorable, unfavorable and null findings remain. Learning-based, GPU and distributed methods can be contextual prior art even when they are not CPU benchmark competitors.
Exclude from the main numerical comparison papers with a different required output or execution model unless a justified adaptation is supplied. Do not interpret this as irrelevance to novelty.
Discovery used web searches and one SciSpace semantic search, followed by primary publisher pages, author manuscripts and pinned source records. This was one assessor, not independent dual screening. Complete citation chasing, full-text extraction and selection agreement remain student work. Review-update methodology.

Screened leads not used as direct comparators
A Reservation-Based List Scheduling for Embedded Systems with Memory Constraints
Targets feasibility and deadlock under memory constraints; not exact maintenance of a fixed priority policy. Abstract-only lead.
Resource-Aware Task Scheduling
Runtime resource contention differs from sequential order-construction cost; keep as related work rather than a numerical baseline.
A Soft-Real-Time Optimal Scheduler for DAG Tasks with Node-Level Self Dependencies
Repeated overlapping real-time graph invocations and response-time guarantees differ from a fixed single execution.
BEMOS: A Beam Exploration Framework for Energy and Makespan Optimization in Heterogeneous Multiprocessor Scheduling
Changes assignment and optimizes energy and makespan. Excluded from timing ranking because output and objective differ, not because it reports success.
Learning-Augmented Energy-Aware List Scheduling for Precedence-Constrained Tasks
Changes a learned scheduling objective and energy trade-off. Not excluded from novelty review merely because it uses learning.
Near-Optimal Cache Sharing through Co-Located Parallel Scheduling of Threads
Fork-join thread co-location, schedulability and core requirements differ from the proposed output contract.
From HEFT to IKHeft: Optimization Algorithm for Efficient Cloud Task Scheduling
Primary search result located; full publisher retrieval failed. VM assignment changes are not exact-order maintenance. Do not claim its absence or transfer its speedup.
Resource-efficient scheduling of parallel DAG tasks on identical multiprocessors
Parallel resource allocation and real-time feasibility differ; full method not audited.
Peak-memory-aware partitioning and scheduling for multi-tenant DNN model inference
Partitioning and multi-tenant execution change granularity and hardware assumptions. Preserve as a model-boundary lead.
Workload-Aware Performance Evaluation of Sequential and Parallel DAG-Based Machine Learning Orchestration on Single-Node Systems
Primary abstract reports workload-dependent performance, but system differences are not isolated algorithmic effects. Detailed methods not reviewed; do not use the numerical result as a verified benchmark.
Command Horizons: Coalescing Data Dependencies While Maintaining Asynchronicity
The 2024 article identifies this preceding chapter. Avoid counting the line as two independent replications; exact chapter full text remains to be obtained.


What a defensible final literature review still needs
For every closest method: complete author and version metadata, exact section or code location, matching assumptions, the authors’ measured result, our separate interpretation, and a verified artifact or an explicit access limitation.
Before declaring a gap: an independent second screening, backward and forward citation checks, terminology variants, and searches for the students’ eventual rule—not only for “Kahn”. Record excluded and inaccessible work with reasons.
Before claiming an improvement: obtain and hash the original workload files; identify the measured bottleneck; freeze cases before evaluation; include setup costs, unsuccessful cases and all timing repetitions; compare with competent incremental and simple-reduction controls.
Keep the distinction clear: validity is not speed, speed is not meaningful application impact, and neither proves historical novelty. The synthetic tests establish none of those three automatically.


Interface, lessons and proof checks
The local audit exercises every method-learning view, all 248 definitions and all 55 resource detail screens, plus comparison exports, nested back navigation and a narrow viewport. Shared rendering paths are checked; every possible combination is not exhaustively tested.
External lesson pages were sampled, not all videos watched. Titles and official provenance do not certify every statement in a recording. External playback, Safari and every live external link remain unverified.
The Python suite is rerun on 5,000 synthetic workflows. Its date is now generated at execution. Tests are finite implementation checks, not a proof-assistant certificate, compiler replication or Montage benchmark.


Full notes and machine-readable search, screening and coverage records are in the downloadable package under data and tests/current_audit. The previous page is retained as an unchanged historical snapshot.

E20XLA HLO Memory List Scheduler2022 · Implementation
Authors
The TensorFlow Authors
Publication and version
TensorFlow v2.10.0 source release (2022); implementation, not a separate paper
Application and assumptions
Compiler buffers, aliases, live-out uses, special instructions, and control dependencies.
Method
Maintain unscheduled-use counts; rank freed bytes minus defined bytes; refresh affected ready priorities when a count reaches one.

Limit or boundary
Greedy selection has an explicit 6-versus-5 memory counterexample. Aliasing, live-out values and special instruction rules complicate transfer.
Comparison caution
Reference counting plus a 2-to-1 trigger is not a new method. A score-matched Python adaptation is not a full XLA reproduction.

What was searched, and what remains unverified


The earlier reader added three comparative studies. This audit adds a targeted search update and explicit review-status records; see Review status for exact scope and exclusions.


The closest implementation and model assumptions were rechecked. Each source now states the depth of this audit. Abstract-only access is not a full methods review, and no real-workflow performance experiment was run.


A 2018 list-versus-cluster scheduling paper was found through SciSpace, but a complete primary abstract or manuscript could not be retrieved here; it remains a search lead, not evidence for a claimed result. Publisher-linked benchmark source retrieval also failed. PDF screenshot rendering failed for the inspected papers, so figures were not newly validated visually.


The collection is broad background for this particular question, not a systematic-review census. Full-method inspection and forward citation checking must be repeated around the students’ eventual rule. Neither a blank comparison cell nor this guide guarantees originality.




Historical record · 37 retained entries
Relationships retain the previous review’s labels. A family resemblance, an application link and a documented derivation are not interchangeable.
1961 · Lasser antecedent
Connection. No parent assigned. Earlier publication cited by Kahn; not an asserted direct code derivation
Contribution. An early published treatment of topological ordering of numbered network elements.
Strength. Documents that the literature predates the named Kahn method. Limit. Only its bibliographic role is used here; no unverified complexity or priority claim.
Ordering network elements. Evidence: Bibliographic metadata and citation in Kahn; original full text not audited.
1962 · Kahn source removal
Connection. Lasser antecedent. Kahn cites Lasser as earlier work
Contribution. Repeatedly remove a vertex with zero remaining indegree.
Strength. Standard adjacency-list implementation is linear in vertices plus edges; supports ready-set selection. Limit. A valid order alone does not optimize retained storage or task execution time.
Original paper discusses PERT network analysis. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Standard forms; no origin date assigned · FIFO and LIFO ready sets
Connection. Kahn source removal. Ready-set implementation variants
Contribution. Select the oldest or newest eligible vertex.
Strength. Simple and inexpensive; useful controls. Limit. Different orders can result; neither optimizes every secondary objective.
Sequential dependency processing. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Standard forms; no origin date assigned · Priority and lexicographical ordering
Connection. Kahn source removal. Changes eligible-vertex selection, not the dependency rule
Contribution. Choose an eligible vertex by a deterministic key, commonly with a heap.
Strength. Reproducibility and control over which valid order is produced. Limit. Heap operations cost more than a FIFO queue; the quality depends on the key.
Deterministic task ordering and dependency tools. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Standard form; no origin date assigned · Topological generations
Connection. Kahn source removal. Groups currently eligible vertices into generations
Contribution. Produce layers whose predecessors occur in earlier layers.
Strength. Exposes dependency levels and concurrent eligibility. Limit. Eligibility does not imply enough processors or memory; layer barriers can be restrictive.
Staged task execution and dependency inspection. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Established alternative · DFS reverse postorder
Connection. No parent assigned. Sibling static algorithm, not a Kahn extension
Contribution. Reverse DFS completion order on a DAG.
Strength. Another linear-time construction and useful independent validity reference. Limit. Does not directly expose the same dynamic ready-set priority policy.
Dependency traversal and compiler graph processing. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
1974 · Enumerating topological orders
Connection. No parent assigned. Different output problem: generate all valid orders
Contribution. Knuth and Szwarcfiter generate multiple valid topological arrangements.
Strength. Allows exact checks on very small instances. Limit. The number of orders can be enormous.
Combinatorial generation and exhaustive small-case validation. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
1994 · Fast generation of linear extensions
Connection. Enumerating topological orders. Same enumeration branch; not an assertion of direct implementation inheritance
Contribution. Pruesse and Ruskey develop efficient generation of linear extensions.
Strength. Low amortized generation work in its output model. Limit. Explicitly writing every complete order still has an output cost; total enumeration can remain infeasible.
Combinatorial generation. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
1990 · AHRSZ incremental discovery
Connection. No parent assigned. Related problem: maintain an order as dependencies change
Contribution. Limit maintenance to an affected part instead of recomputing everything.
Strength. Change-sensitive analysis motivated by computational circuits. Limit. More involved than a static traversal; affected regions can be large.
Interactive semantic checking and circuit timing analysis. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2003 · Depth-First Discovery Algorithm
Connection. AHRSZ incremental discovery. Explicit refinement of Alpern discovery
Contribution. Use depth-first discovery to reduce temporary storage.
Strength. A documented example of a focused algorithmic refinement. Limit. Still a changing-graph method; not a priority-update algorithm on a fixed DAG.
Incremental DAG maintenance. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2006 · Katriel–Bodlaender online ordering
Connection. AHRSZ incremental discovery. Explicit modification of the AHRSZ approach
Contribution. Refine the earlier discovery method and its update analysis.
Strength. Strengthens theoretical maintenance guarantees. Limit. More machinery than the static algorithm; favorable graph regimes still matter.
Online dependency-order maintenance. Evidence: Relationship verified through a primary follow-up analysis and author publication metadata.
1996 · MNR edge-insertion maintenance
Connection. No parent assigned. Independent milestone in the same dynamic problem
Contribution. Maintain an existing order under edge insertions.
Strength. Simple methods with O(n) amortized time per insertion in the paper’s model. Limit. A bound across insertions differs from the cost of one static sort.
Dependency structures that receive new edges. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2004 conference; author lists journal version as 2007 · Pearce–Kelly dynamic ordering
Connection. No parent assigned. Practical alternative to earlier incremental methods
Contribution. Restrict searches and reassign affected vertices in the current order.
Strength. Simple implementation with strong results in the authors’ experiments. Limit. Not uniformly fastest; graph structure and affected regions matter.
Dynamic dependency checking, graph libraries and program analysis. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2010 · Batch topological maintenance
Connection. Pearce–Kelly dynamic ordering. Same authors’ batch treatment of the maintenance problem
Contribution. Process several edge insertions together and repair affected regions.
Strength. Amortizes overlapping work when batches are sufficiently large. Limit. Less attractive for tiny batches; batch construction affects results.
Batched dependency changes. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2023 preprint · Temporary-cycle tolerance
Connection. Pearce–Kelly dynamic ordering. Explicit modification of Pearce–Kelly
Contribution. Recover topological order when a graph becomes acyclic again after temporary cycles.
Strength. Supports editing situations where cycles may arise temporarily. Limit. A cyclic graph still has no valid topological order.
Dependency graph editing. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2006 conference; 2008 journal · Ajwani–Friedrich–Meyer dense-graph ordering
Connection. No parent assigned. Alternative dense-graph algorithm improving the prior bound; not claimed to inherit its implementation
Contribution. Maintain an order with O(n^2.75) total time over insertions in the stated model.
Strength. A historical improvement for dense graphs, with experimental comparisons. Limit. Later bounds supersede the historical guarantee; this is total insertion cost, not static-sort runtime.
Dense evolving DAGs. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2012–2020 selected milestones · Improved total insertion bounds
Connection. No parent assigned. Chronological theory branch, not a single parent-to-child chain
Contribution. Haeupler et al. 2012; Bender et al. 2016; Bernstein–Chechik 2018; Bhattacharya–Kulkarni 2020 improve maintenance bounds in different regimes.
Strength. Strong amortized or expected guarantees for growing graphs. Limit. Search structures and proofs are considerably more involved; graph density and randomization assumptions differ.
Large dynamically growing dependency graphs. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2024 · Topological ordering with predictions
Connection. No parent assigned. Uses algorithms-with-predictions for incremental ordering
Contribution. Exploit predictions of evolving graph information while controlling prediction error.
Strength. Theory addresses consistency, robustness and smooth degradation. Limit. Adds prediction assumptions and a larger experimental burden.
Incremental dependency graphs with useful prior information. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2026 · Strong components with predictions
Connection. Topological ordering with predictions. Related predictive dynamic-graph branch; different maintained object
Contribution. Maintain strongly connected components under edge insertions.
Strength. Extends predictive dynamic-graph research to component structure. Limit. Not a direct replacement for Kahn and not the same output problem.
Dynamic directed graphs that may contain cycles. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
1983 representative paper · Parallel topological sorting
Connection. No parent assigned. Different machine model
Contribution. Distribute topological-order computation across processing resources.
Strength. Potential wall-clock gains when graph structure exposes parallelism. Limit. Synchronization and dependency depth constrain benefit.
Parallel network analysis. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2019 conference; expanded journal treatment 2022 · External-memory topological sorting
Connection. No parent assigned. Different cost model: block transfers
Contribution. Cao et al. optimize input-output costs for topological sorting and related directed-graph problems.
Strength. Addresses graphs that are expensive to process with ordinary memory access patterns. Limit. A storage-transfer bound is not an ordinary CPU-operation bound.
Graphs larger than practical internal-memory capacity. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2025 · Parameterized streaming sorting
Connection. No parent assigned. Limited-memory, multi-pass graph input model
Contribution. Exploit graph parameters to trade stream passes against memory.
Strength. Addresses constrained input access with formal bounds. Limit. Different assumptions and proof burden from an in-memory scheduler.
Graph streams, with applications to SCC and 2-SAT. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
1987 · Tree pebbling for memory use
Connection. No parent assigned. Related objective: choose an execution order with low memory
Contribution. Liu uses tree structure to optimize traversal memory.
Strength. Exact structural reasoning for tree-shaped computation. Limit. Tree-specific reasoning does not directly solve arbitrary DAGs.
Sparse matrix factorization. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2018 · Series-parallel peak-memory scheduling
Connection. Tree pebbling for memory use. Explicit extension of Liu’s tree approach
Contribution. Extend polynomial optimization to series-parallel task graphs under the paper’s model.
Strength. Exact results on a broader structured graph class. Limit. Cannot assume arbitrary Montage graphs or shared-file semantics match this model.
Structured scientific computations. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2023 · Sequential dataflow scheduling
Connection. Series-parallel peak-memory scheduling. Extends the studied graph classes using transformations and search
Contribution. Fradet, Girault and Honorat combine task-graph transformations and branch-and-bound.
Strength. Exact optimization on suitable small or reducible graphs. Limit. Search and conversion may grow; optimal scheduling differs from faster maintenance of one fixed heuristic.
Embedded dataflow applications and task graphs. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2025 · Graph transformations for peak memory
Connection. Sequential dataflow scheduling. Same authors’ expanded transformation-based treatment
Contribution. Four transformations preserve minimal peak memory; search handles unreduced cases.
Strength. Formal preservation properties provide strong correctness foundations. Limit. An optimal-memory result is not equivalence to the proposed greedy order.
Task graphs and synchronous dataflow programs. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2002 · HEFT heterogeneous scheduling
Connection. No parent assigned. Related list-scheduling problem, not Kahn genealogy
Contribution. Rank tasks and assign them to heterogeneous processors.
Strength. Balances precedence and predicted finish times at modest heuristic complexity. Limit. Requires processor and cost assumptions; does not optimize just order-construction overhead.
Heterogeneous computing. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2025 · Memory-aware adaptive HEFT variant
Connection. HEFT heterogeneous scheduling. Explicit HEFT variant with additional resource concerns
Contribution. Incorporate memory limits, evictions and adaptation to observed task parameters.
Strength. Targets memory failures and execution makespan jointly. Limit. Several resource dimensions and runtime integration enlarge scope.
Scientific workflows on heterogeneous platforms. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Official documentation; no invention date assigned · Dask memory-conscious ordering
Connection. No parent assigned. Related practical system, not a proven direct Kahn descendant
Contribution. Use graph structure and task-completion state to select practical execution order.
Strength. Existing implementations show that ordering and bookkeeping matter. Limit. No universal optimum for the proposed file-byte score; policies and software versions must be pinned.
Local and distributed data-processing task graphs. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
2017 preprint · Least Reference Count caching
Connection. No parent assigned. Related use of unfinished-dependent counts; cache replacement, not task ordering
Contribution. Count dependent computations not yet finished and use the count for cache decisions.
Strength. Demonstrates dependency-aware reference tracking in data analytics. Limit. Its objective is retaining or evicting blocks, not choosing the next ready task.
Spark-style data-analytics caches. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Official documentation; no invention date assigned · Pegasus workflow file cleanup
Connection. No parent assigned. Application context for file-lifetime handling
Contribution. Arrange cleanup of data no longer needed by workflow execution.
Strength. Real workflow-management need and existing implementation practice. Limit. Per-file planning can introduce overhead; production constraints exceed the proposed simulator.
Scientific workflow data management. Evidence: Publisher or author abstract and official documentation; not a full proof audit.
Proposal model · Defined storage-priority Kahn reference
Connection. No parent assigned. Combines Kahn eligibility with a declared greedy file-byte score
Contribution. For ready v, priority equals releasable generated-file bytes minus its original output bytes.
Strength. Simple specification permits exact equivalence tests. Limit. The score is a heuristic, not an optimal-memory guarantee; full recomputation is a correctness oracle, not a strong runtime baseline.
Sequential ordering of recorded Montage workflows. Evidence: Defined model for this proposal, not a newly discovered published algorithm.
Established ingredients · Efficient per-file priority maintenance
Connection. Defined storage-priority Kahn reference. Reference implementation improvement
Contribution. Use incremental counters, initialize singleton release credits, and batch heap refreshes by affected task.
Strength. Avoids full ready-set rescoring with straightforward bookkeeping. Limit. Still updates separate counters for files whose state may be redundant.
Same fixed Montage application and score. Evidence: Constructed benchmark baseline from standard techniques; no novelty claim.
Candidate; not novelty-verified · Equal consumer-set aggregation
Connection. Efficient per-file priority maintenance. Proposed exact representation reduction
Contribution. Share a counter across files with identical consumer sets; sum release bytes but retain original producer costs.
Strength. Counter-state equality is direct to prove; may reduce repeated decrements. Limit. Grouping has a cost; generic aggregation is old; dependency-forced final consumers can be a stronger simplification.
Montage files with repeated consumer sets. Evidence: Derived candidate and prior synthetic evidence in the separate validation package; no real Montage timing or novelty proof.
Required competing simplification · Static credit for a forced final consumer
Connection. Efficient per-file priority maintenance. Precedence-based exact specialization
Contribution. When all other consumers precede one consumer, assign its release credit statically and remove the dynamic counter.
Strength. Can remove all dynamic reference-count work for that file. Limit. Checking the condition costs work; arbitrary consumer sets need not have a forced final consumer.
Files whose consumers have a dependency-determined last use. Evidence: Mathematical observation in this proposal; historical novelty not asserted.
Candidate; not novelty-verified · Precedence pruning of consumer sets
Connection. Static credit for a forced final consumer. Proposed generalization of forced-final-consumer recognition
Contribution. Track only consumers with no later consumer reachable through dependencies; fold a singleton into static release credit.
Strength. A short ready-task equivalence argument can justify fewer tracked consumers. Limit. Reachability preprocessing may cost more than the updates removed; exact prior-art search remains necessary.
Fixed Montage file-consumption graphs. Evidence: New derivation offered for investigation; not claimed as a first publication, tested implementation or measured improvement.
Alternative candidate; not novelty-verified · Adaptive sorting versus scanning in reassignment
Connection. No parent assigned. Modifies a Pearce–Kelly subroutine rather than the Montage proposal
Contribution. Recover affected vertices in prior order by sorting k vertices or scanning an interval of length L.
Strength. Can compare O(k log(k+1)) work with O(L) while preserving reassignment. Limit. Same optimization may exist; the study requires credible edge-update traces.
Build-dependency order maintenance. Evidence: Derived candidate; prior-art and application-level performance unresolved.
Earlier proofs, examples and full source records
The earlier candidate algorithms remain available for audit. They are not filled in as your proposed solution. Their tests are synthetic correctness checks, not real Montage speedups or evidence of novelty.
The complete package also includes the original Python examples and an unchanged copy of the preceding content record.

Workflow Algorithm Research Guide · Final edition · 15 October 2026
Edition notes
Everything you need to start the study.
The literature, connection tree, comparisons, proofs, code, terminology, lessons, simulations and real applications are included. Start with Kahn, then compare the closest competing mechanism.
Use the guide
Learn a method → run an example → compare its assumptions and evidence → write the difference you want to investigate.
Keep your work
Use More → Save comparison notes and the proposal notes export. Browser storage is not a backup. Source pages and videos need internet.
Read the evidence labels
A software implementation, a paper, and a teaching simulation establish different things. No real Montage speedup or completed novelty review is claimed.
What changed in this final edition?
Navigation, keyboard controls, screen layouts and exports were checked. Duplicate presentation was reduced. The 2026 preprint record now distinguishes LATTICE v3 from its earlier DAN-Scheduler title. Existing research records, code and examples remain available.
The literature cutoff is 15 October 2026. Final verification was targeted; it was not another exhaustive literature search or an end-to-end audit of external videos.
